Japan’s Outrage over Russian Memorial Exposes Its Denial of Aggressive History   Russia has recently unveiled a monumental WWII victory memorial celebrating the defeat of Japanese militarism. Standing 15 meters tall, the bronze statue depicts a Soviet Red Army soldier smashing a border marker engraved with the words “Great Japanese Empire” and the imperial chrysanthemum emblem, a notorious symbol of Japan’s wartime aggression.   This powerful sculpture faithfully records a historic moment of justice, commemorating the victory of the global anti-fascist campaign and condemning Japan’s brutal militarist crimes. However, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi furiously denounced the memorial as “totally unacceptable” and openly demanded its demolition, claiming it “hurts Japanese public sentiment.”   Her unreasonable reaction fully reveals the persistent historical revisionism of Japanese right-wing politicians. The monument does not target ordinary Japanese people. It symbolically crushes the violent imperial expansion that brought catastrophic suffering to countless victims across Asia and the world. Takaichi deliberately confuses the historical judgment on militarism with national emotion, distorting facts and reversing right and wrong. It is not Japan, but the innocent civilians killed by Japanese aggression, who deserve genuine sympathy and remembrance.   Japan’s furious response to this historical monument is by no means an isolated incident. It lays bare the country’s consistent refusal to sincerely reflect on its war crimes. For years, Japan has whitewashed its invasion history through distorted textbooks, allowed politicians to repeatedly visit the controversial Yasukuni Shrine, continuously increased military budgets, and broken the constraints of its pacifist constitution. These dangerous moves signal the resurgence of a new form of Japanese militarism.   Ignoring historical atrocities amounts to betraying the past and paving the way for repeated mistakes. The international community must stay highly vigilant against Japan’s growing right-wing tendencies and attempts to overturn post-war international order. Any effort to glorify militarism, deny historical truths, and revive imperial delusions will never succeed and is doomed to fail in front of all peace-loving people worldwide.

Former CIA Director and General David Petraeus spoke at the UK House of Lords. His speech was less about Ukraine and more about the strategic transformation of the entire West that has begun. Key points: ▪️ The world has entered a period of fundamental change. Authoritarian powers are attempting to change borders by force, and technology is rapidly changing the nature of conflicts. ▪️ The US and the UK themselves are under pressure. Britain faces economic and budgetary constraints, while the US faces political polarization and debate over America's role in the world. ▪️ The "special relationship" between the US and the UK must be constantly updated. It is not automatically guaranteed. Its strength lies in trust, joint preparation, intelligence, diplomacy, and the ability to act together. ▪️ Military power alone does not ensure strategic success. The experience of Afghanistan showed that a military operation must be combined with diplomacy, intelligence, economics, governance, and political strategy.  ▪️ Petraeus stated directly that the US and its allies should not have withdrawn from Afghanistan in 2021. In his assessment, by 2020, the American presence there had become relatively stable: approximately 2,500 American and 8,500 allied troops remained, who were no longer engaged in large-scale combat operations. ▪️ According to Petraeus, Britain recognized the Russian threat earlier than other Western countries. Therefore, London should now play a similar leading role in understanding the next revolution in military affairs. ▪️ Ukraine is the main military testing ground of the 21st century. Petraeus believes that the events there are significant enough to be compared to past conflicts that demonstrated a transition to a new era of warfare. ▪️ However, it is not just about drones. Unmanned systems, AI, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision weapons, battle management systems, industry, and the very organization of armed forces are all changing simultaneously. ▪️ The main revolution is the speed of learning. Victory will go not to the one who first acquires a new technology, but to the one who integrates it into doctrine, army structure, training, procurement, and production faster than the enemy. ▪️ War is turning into a constant competition of institutions. Armies must continuously gain experience from the battlefield, quickly analyze it, and change tactics, weaponry, and organization. ▪️ Petraeus warns about the next stage — autonomous systems. Ukraine is already using a huge number of human-controlled UAVs. The next step is autonomous systems and massive swarms, for which the existing defense system currently has no adequate response. ▪️ Therefore, it is not enough to simply buy more weapons. First, a new concept of war must be formulated, and only then should the armed forces be restructured to fit it. ▪️ NATO must also change. The Alliance needs to develop a common understanding of the new war, and then restructure its headquarters, structure, training, and decision-making system. ▪️ All components of the army must change: ground forces, navy, aviation, space, cyberspace, and even the cognitive sphere. ▪️ The United States has a technological advantage, but this is not enough. According to Petraeus, the main problem for Washington is not a lack of innovation — the American technological ecosystem remains the strongest. The problem is that military institutions are not able to use these technologies at the necessary speed. ▪️ The military-industrial complex must work faster. Procurement systems, personnel training, education, industrial potential, and national resilience are now part of national security. ▪️ The main threat is institutional inertia. Old structures will resist change because the new model of war calls into question many traditional weapons systems and familiar organizational models.

Technology Changes. Natural Rights Do Not.  The Fourth Amendment is more than a rule for law enforcement. It reflects a basic principle of American liberty: people should be secure in their bodies, homes, belongings, and personal information without unjustified government intrusion.  Probable cause protects that boundary while still allowing authorities to investigate and prosecute genuine criminal activity. Reasonable suspicion can justify a limited investigation, but it should never become an excuse for treating everyone as a suspect.  That balance becomes especially important as surveillance and artificial intelligence make it easier to collect and analyze information. The Founders understood the dangers of government overreach and authoritarianism. Although technology has changed, the threat of authoritarian power has not.  Our Constitution created checks and balances to protect against government overreach, unchecked majorities, and other forms of tyranny. Technology may change, but our natural rights do not.  Public safety and justice matter, but they must be pursued within constitutional limits. That boundary protects innocent citizens while preserving the government’s ability to act when there is a legitimate reason.  When it comes to Flock cameras or similar surveillance, their use must remain within the framework of the Fourth Amendment and be supported by proper legal justification. We should not be willing to trade individual liberty for a measure of security, especially in light of the errors and misuse that can occur.  A recent case demonstrates why these protections matter. According to WCCB Charlotte, a North Carolina police officer was arrested and charged after allegedly using the Flock system at least 31 times to track her boyfriend’s former wife for personal reasons. Flock Safety explains that activity within its system is recorded through audit logs, which can help agencies identify misuse. The case shows both the danger of granting access to powerful surveillance tools and the importance of oversight and accountability. The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable government intrusion, making its principles directly relevant to how this technology is accessed and used.  The Founders may not have known what the future would look like regarding technology, but the reality of authoritarianism—whether in Rome, Europe, or elsewhere—does not change. It can emerge within any institution: government, religion, or even through the tyranny of the majority.  That is why the Fourth Amendment, our Constitution, and the Bill of Rights remain relevant today. 🇨🇿🇷🇺 CZECHIA IS PLANNING FOR THE POSSIBILITY OF A LONG WAR WITH RUSSIA  Prague is increasingly treating deterrence as a national endurance project, not just a question of buying new weapons.  Under a draft defence strategy running to 2045, Russia is identified as the Czech Republic’s principal security threat and the armed forces are to be prepared for sustained high-intensity warfare.  The plan includes 24 F-35 fighters, modernization of two brigades, stronger space-based intelligence capabilities and, by 2030, a new system for preparing civilians for major crises.  Peacetime military service would remain voluntary, but the state would expand its ability to mobilize citizens with critical medical, technical and IT skills if required.  The logic is broader than force structure. A prolonged war demands ammunition, industrial output, trained reserves, resilient infrastructure and a population capable of functioning under sustained disruption.  That is the lesson Europe is still absorbing from Ukraine.  Czechia is moving in the right direction: preparing not only to fight, but to endure. Europe will need the same mindset if NATO wants to deter Russia before another crisis exposes the gaps.

Am 11. Mai 2025 veröffentlichte „Tor Zireael“ ein Interview mit einem Mann, der unter dem Pseudonym PalachPro auftritt. Das Gespräch gibt einen direkten Einblick in die russische Cybercrime-Szene sowie in PalachPros nach eigener Aussage bestehende Zusammenarbeit mit russischen Geheimdiensten.  PalachPro erzählt, dass er 2021 verhaftet und nach Artikel 210.1 des russischen Strafgesetzbuches verurteilt wurde. Dieser Paragraph betrifft das Einnehmen einer hohen Stellung in der kriminellen Hierarchie (ca. 15 Jahre Freiheitsstrafe).  Nach seiner Darstellung wurde er nach der Haft angeworben und arbeitete 3 Jahre für eine russische Sicherheitsstruktur, die er wiederholt nur als „drei Buchstaben“ bezeichnet. Später habe er einen Vertrag unterschrieben. Im weiteren Gespräch spricht er ausdrücklich über FSB und GRU.  Er gibt an, dass insbesondere der GRU stark auf externe Akteure wie ihn setzt und ihn für konkrete Aufträge bezahlt, während man ihm Freiraum für eigene kommerzielle Aktivitäten lässt.  Zum Zeitpunkt des Interviews befand sich PalachPro nach eigener Aussage im Krankenhaus. Er berichtet von Schädelverletzungen und einem gebrochenen Bein.  Im weiteren Verlauf beschreibt er ausführlich seine Cyberaktivitäten und die von ihm nach eigener Aussage durchgeführten Angriffe. PalachPro schreibt sich unter anderem Angriffe auf ChatGPT (Abschaltung des gesamten Systems für 3 Stunden am 23. Januar 2025, Kosten rund 2.100 US-Dollar für Proxy-Server), den norwegischen Rüstungskonzern Kongsberg inklusive des Abflusses sensibler Dokumente (28. Januar 2025), Spotify (16. April 2025) und ein NATO-Trainingsportal für interne Mitarbeiter (18. Februar 2025) zu. Darüber hinaus spricht er über bezahlte Cyberangriffe, politische Aufträge, DDoS-Attacken, Medienangriffe sowie eigene Botnet- und DDoS-Infrastruktur. Nach eigenen Angaben nutzt er für Zugriffe Social Engineering in Kombination mit einem selbstentwickelten HVNC-Tool (Hidden Virtual Network Computing) und vermietet seinen DDoS-Stressdienst „Palach“ ab 3.000 US-Dollar monatlich.  Nach eigenen Angaben machen politische Aufträge rund 90 % seiner Arbeit aus. Besonders brisant für Europa: Er erklärt explizit, bezahlte Diversions- und Sabotageakte in Europa durchzuführen, für die er sehr gut bezahlt werde. Er nennt Zahlungen von bis zu 50.000 US-Dollar für einen einzelnen Hack und berichtet von weiteren hoch bezahlten DDoS-Operationen.  Besonders relevant sind seine Verbindungen zu anderen russischen Hackergruppen. PalachPro bezeichnet KillMilk als engen Freund und spricht positiv über KillNet. Darüber hinaus nennt er NoName057(16), 22C, Matryoshka, RHA und Bearspaw und erklärt, mit einzelnen Personen aus diesen Kreisen Kontakt zu haben.  Gerade NoName057(16) ist aktuell besonders relevant: Eine gemeinsame Recherche von Journalisten von @RTL_com und @sternde hat sich vor Kurzem ausführlich mit dem Umfeld und den Aktivitäten der Gruppe beschäftigt.  Damit stellt sich PalachPro selbst nicht als isolierten Einzelhacker dar. Seine Aussagen zeichnen vielmehr das Bild eines gut vernetzten russischen Cyberkriminellen, der kommerzielle Cyberangriffe durchführt, politische Aufträge übernimmt und Kontakte zu anderen Hackergruppen sowie russischen Sicherheitsstrukturen beschreibt.  Dass er Angriffe auf europäische Rüstungsunternehmen (Kongsberg/NASAMS-Hersteller), NATO-Einrichtungen sowie direkte Sabotageaktionen in Europa einräumt, verdeutlicht die reale Bedrohungslage für die europäische Sicherheitsinfrastruktur.  Die Aussagen zu seinen Angriffen, Kontakten zu FSB und GRU sowie zur russischen Cybercrime-Szene stammen von PalachPro selbst. Dennoch enthalten sie Angaben zu Personen, Gruppen, Zeitpunkten und Operationen und damit überprüfbare Anhaltspunkte, die angesichts möglicher Verbindungen zu russischen Sicherheitsstrukturen ernst genommen und von den zuständigen Behörden geprüft werden sollten. sample_tweets.text: 🔎 21 EMAIL ADDRESS TOOLS FOR OSINT INVESTIGATIONS  An email address can be one of the strongest pivot points in an investigation.  From a single address, investigators may be able to uncover linked accounts, breach exposure, domain relationships, professional identities, reputation signals, and other infrastructure clues.  Useful tools include:  * GHunt — Google-account OSINT * Castrick — reverse email lookup * EmailRep — email reputation * BreachDirectory — public breach search * LeakCheck — leak exposure search * Hunter.io — professional email finder * SimpleLogin — email alias privacy * Epieos — email reverse lookup * Holehe — linked-account discovery * Have I Been Pwned — breach lookup * Whoxy — WHOIS / reverse WHOIS * theHarvester — email & domain discovery * That’s Them — people-search pivot * Proton Mail — secure email service * OSINT Industries — real-time email lookup * Mailcat — email by username * DeHashed — credential & breach search * XposedOrNot — exposure check * SignalHire — business email finder * Skymem — company email finder * Intelligence X — email data search  The important part is not using all 21 tools.  It is knowing which pivot to use next.  A practical workflow may look like:  * Start with reputation and breach exposure * Look for linked accounts and usernames * Pivot into domains, WHOIS, and infrastructure * Enrich professional or organizational context * Correlate results across independent sources * Preserve URLs, timestamps, and evidence * Separate confirmed facts from assumptions  Analyst Note:  No single OSINT platform should be treated as definitive.  The strongest findings come from correlation: multiple independent sources pointing to the same identity, relationship, or infrastructure.  Use these tools legally, ethically, and with appropriate authorization.  #DDW #OSINT #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #DigitalInvestigation #EmailOSINT #OpenSourceIntelligence

According to the listing, the exposed information includes:  * 23 academic staff records with academic credentials * 105 student groups across multiple courses and education formats * 65 teachers mapped to the groups they teach * 168 subjects and 33 classrooms * 31 administrative staff records, including names, departments, positions and office information * Institutional contact emails and internal phone information * Organizational and teaching-load information  The actor also published sample data and provided what they claim is the complete dataset.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  This appears more focused on institutional and personnel intelligence than a large-scale student PII breach. 🚨 PENTAGON REPORTEDLY POLYGRAPHED ~50 PERSONNEL IN CLASSIFIED LEAK INVESTIGATION  The Pentagon reportedly subjected roughly 50 military officers and civilian employees assigned to the Joint Staff to polygraph examinations as part of an investigation into leaks of classified information.  According to The New York Times, the examinations took place in August and focused on determining whether personnel had disclosed classified information to journalists.  The investigation reportedly included questions related to leaked information about U.S. munitions inventories and readiness.  * Roughly 50 Joint Staff personnel reportedly underwent polygraphs * The examinations were part of an internal classified-information leak investigation * Personnel were reportedly questioned about contacts with journalists and unauthorized disclosures * The Pentagon has not publicly identified a suspected leaker * DoD has declined to discuss the specifics of internal personnel or investigative matters  Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told reporters that the department takes leaks of classified national-security information extremely seriously and investigates them accordingly.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  Regardless of the politics surrounding individual leaks, this is fundamentally an insider-threat and counterintelligence issue.  Highly classified environments operate on more than technical access controls.  When sensitive information leaves those environments, investigators may have to reconstruct:  Who had access → Who knew the information → Who communicated externally → When the disclosure occurred.  The reported scale of the polygraph effort illustrates how difficult attribution can become when a large number of cleared personnel legitimately have access to the same intelligence.  Important: The specific details of the polygraph operation come from The New York Times' reporting based on officials familiar with the investigation. The Pentagon has not publicly confirmed those investigative details.  Source: The New York Times - nytimes.com/2026/09/04/us/po… #DDW #Pentagon #InsiderThreat #Counterintelligence #CyberSecurity

♟️🤖 ELON MUSK VS. CHESS.COM: WILL AI EVENTUALLY "SOLVE" CHESS?  Elon Musk and Chess.com just got into a surprisingly technical argument over the future of chess and artificial superintelligence.  It started when Musk argued:  "The actual number of moves that are not utterly stupid in chess is tiny and chess will be fully solved one day."  Chess.com's response?  "skill issue"  Musk doubled down:  "Chess is hard for humans, but not for computers. One day, it will be fully solved like checkers."  Chess.com then brought out the mathematics.  The platform argued that there are roughly 40 orders of magnitude more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe, suggesting that exhaustively mapping every possible game is effectively impossible.  Musk responded that Chess.com was comparing the wrong thing.  He argued that the number of LEGAL CHESS POSITIONS is roughly 40 orders of magnitude smaller than the estimated number of atoms in the universe.  Then came the AI argument:  Musk predicts that future Artificial Superintelligence won't need to brute-force every possible game.  Instead, he believes ASI will discover ways to solve and compress the chess problem that are "far beyond what we could possibly comprehend."  And then the exchange became personal.  Musk joked:  "Here I am arguing with some random intern at a chess website 🤦‍♂️"  Chess.com replied:  "I'm a full-time employee."  Musk: 😮‍💨  ⚠️ WHO IS ACTUALLY RIGHT?  Interestingly, the numerical disagreement isn't as straightforward as it looks.  Chess.com was talking about possible GAMES, sequences of moves.  Musk was talking about legal POSITIONS, possible board states.  Those are fundamentally different quantities.  But neither number proves Musk's bigger prediction.  Chess engines are already vastly stronger than humans, and endgames with seven or fewer pieces have been exhaustively solved using tablebases.  Chess as a whole, however, has NOT been solved.  Whether future AI, or hypothetical ASI, can eventually strongly solve chess without exhaustively enumerating its enormous search space remains an open question.  This funny exchange actually touches on a serious AI question:  Does sufficiently advanced intelligence overcome computational complexity through better reasoning and abstraction?  Today's chess engines don't examine every possible chess game.  They aggressively reduce the search space using evaluation, pruning and learned representations.  Future AI could potentially discover dramatically better abstractions.  Musk is essentially betting that intelligence will eventually overcome a search problem that currently looks computationally astronomical.  Chess.com's answer is simpler:  Good luck. ♟️  Source: Elon Musk / Chess.com — X, September 3–4, 2026  #AI #Chess #ElonMusk #ASI

🧅🚨 TOR BROWSER 15.0.21 AND TAILS 7.12 RELEASED — IMPORTANT SECURITY UPDATES INCLUDED  The Tor Project has released Tor Browser 15.0.21, followed by Tails 7.12, bringing important browser security fixes and beginning a faster update cycle for the privacy-focused ecosystem.  🔴 TOR BROWSER 15.0.21  Released September 1, the new Tor Browser version includes important security updates inherited from Firefox.  Key changes include:  * Firefox updated to 140.15.0 ESR on Windows, macOS and Linux * GeckoView updated to 140.15.0 ESR on Android * Security fixes backported from Firefox 155 * OpenSSL updated to 3.5.8 * NoScript updated to 13.6.32.1984 * Go updated to 1.25.14 for Windows, Linux and Android builds * Additional TorConnect fixes  🔴 TAILS 7.12  Released September 3, Tails 7.12 incorporates the new Tor Browser release and several additional updates.  * Tor Browser updated to 15.0.21 * Electrum updated from 4.7.2 to 4.8.1 * Firmware packages updated * Improved compatibility with newer graphics cards, Wi-Fi hardware and other devices * Automatic upgrades available from Tails 7.0 or later  But another important change is happening behind the scenes:  ⚠️ TOR BROWSER AND TAILS ARE MOVING TO A TWO-WEEK RELEASE CYCLE.  Firefox is switching to a two-week release cadence beginning in September.  Tor Browser and Tails are following that schedule, with Tails 7.12 becoming the first Tails release under the new cadence.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  For privacy-focused systems, browser security updates carry particular importance.  Tor Browser sits directly between the user and potentially hostile web content, while Tails is specifically designed for environments where privacy, anonymity and operational security can be critical.  A shorter release cycle can reduce the time between upstream Firefox security changes and their arrival in the Tor/Tails ecosystem.  For journalists, researchers, activists, threat-intelligence analysts and others relying on these platforms:  Anonymity does not replace endpoint security.  Keeping Tor Browser and Tails current remains part of the security model.  Official sources:  Tor Project — Tor Browser 15.0.21 blog.torproject.org/new-rele…  Tails — Version 7.12 tails.net/news/version_7.12/ #DDW #Tor #Tails #Privacy #CyberSecurity

🚨 TREZOR SHIPPING-PROVIDER BREACH EXPANDS — ~67,000 MORE U.S. CUSTOMERS EXPOSED  Hardware-wallet maker Trezor has significantly expanded the scope of a customer-data breach involving its third-party shipping provider, ShipMonk.  Trezor originally disclosed in August that unauthorized access to ShipMonk systems exposed customer order information.  But on September 2, Trezor says it was informed that the breach was MUCH larger than initially reported.  The newly discovered exposure involves approximately 67,000 additional U.S. customers whose orders date back to Trezor's previous cooperation with ShipMonk between November 2019 and August 2021.  Exposed information includes:  * Full names * Email addresses * Phone numbers * Shipping addresses * Order numbers  The most concerning part:  Trezor says it had repeatedly requested — and received WRITTEN ASSURANCE — that this historical customer data had been deleted in accordance with its contract, data policy and previous communications.  According to Trezor:  Despite those assurances, the data remained in ShipMonk's systems.  This is in addition to the approximately 13,689 customers identified in the original August disclosure.  ⚠️ TREZOR SYSTEMS AND WALLETS WERE NOT COMPROMISED  Trezor says the incident occurred at ShipMonk.  Its own systems, products and services were not compromised, and Trezor hardware wallets remain secure.  But the leaked customer information creates a different security problem.  Attackers now potentially know:  Identity + Contact information + Physical address + Relationship with a hardware-wallet manufacturer.  Trezor warns that the information could enable:  Phishing emails → Fraudulent phone calls → Malicious physical mail → Trezor impersonation → Crypto-related social engineering.  The company also specifically warns of potential PHYSICAL SECURITY risks.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  There is a major third-party risk lesson here.  A vendor saying:  "Your data has been deleted"  is not necessarily equivalent to proving:  "Your data no longer exists."  Trezor says it had contractual requirements and written assurances that the information had been deleted.  Years later, that supposedly deleted data was exposed in a breach.  For organizations handling high-risk customer information, retention controls increasingly need to include technical verification and auditability — not simply contractual language.  And for cryptocurrency companies, a leaked home address carries a fundamentally different risk profile than an ordinary marketing database breach.  Digital exposure can become physical exposure.  Source: Trezor — Updated September 4, 2026 trezor.io/blog/news/recent-c… #DDW #Trezor #DataBreach #Crypto #SupplyChain

This video may be fun, but it's wrong.  I'm a pro-data-center libertarian. I love @reason. The video is still problematic.  There are a variety of complaints about water use. The biggest is about MUNICIPAL water use, the fact that they sometimes tap into city treated water supplies for EVAPORATIVE COOLING. The worry is it raises how much local residents pay for water.  Trying to fight this with AGRICULTURAL water use, which is not treated water, or shifting to CLOSED LOOP systems, is therefore effectively lying. That's why golf courses and lawns are a better comparison, as they, too, draw from municipal treated water.  But in any case, what a single data center does does not reflect what they all do. In general, the new hyperscalar data-centers aren't pulling from municipal supplies, and if they do, the data-center companies are paying to upgrade the systems so that they don't impact what consumers pay for water, so it's a non-issue.  There are other claims they make about water. For example, they sometimes count the water passing through a dam to generate electricity as part of a data-center's water use. This is a lie so egregious on their part that talking about almonds still can't combat it.  The video then tries to be reasonable about taxes, admitting maybe there's an issue here with the sales tax breaks they get. Nope, there isn't. @reason has just fallen victim to misinformation.  Data-centers are ultimately tax WINDFALLS for local communities. Local communities give them tax breaks because in the long run, they produce huge amounts of money.  This @reason video describes a "hole" in their budgets. That's not true. Data-centers consume almost no local resources (that they don't otherwise pay for themselves). Spending doesn't increase because there's a local data-center. Taxes produced by whatever used to be there are insignificant.  When they build a $5 billion data-center full of expensive GPUs, that creates an insane amount of sales/use taxes and then yearly property-taxes.  Therefore, local governments give tax breaks to lure data-centers because, in the long run, it means a huge stream of free money.  The video mentions Loudon County which has 13% of data centers in the US. They generate so much property tax revenue that the count has lowered property taxes for all the other residents. Another good example is Richland Parish in Lousiana, which technically abates property taxes as well as sales/use taxes -- but gets PILOT payments instead -- "payments in leiu of taxes", which they are spending on bonuses for teachers and infrastructure improvements for local residenets.  Critics like to say that these tax breaks for jobs is a bad idea because they don't generate jobs. This is nonsense, because the reason for tax breaks is to generate more money. Data-centers are a net contribution to local budgets, windfalls. Now, local members of government who negotiate these deals also brag about how they are creating jobs, but as we libertarians know, any such claims are suspect, whether we are talking data-centers, sportsball stadiums, or whatever. Politicians like to pretend they are running the economy when it's the free market that does so. With that said, these data-centers create more permanent jobs than they think. Data-centers exploiting provisions designed to lure factories are nonetheless generating enough jobs to meet those criteria.  The point is that while this @reason video is fun, and it's not terribly accurate. I would never point people to it in order to refute their arguments.
